Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Meta Meta says its AI model hacked into another company during testing Company is the third to report such an incident after Anthropic and OpenAI reported breaches during training Reuters Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.27 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Meta said on Wednesday that one of its AI models hacked ⁠another company during cybersecurity testing, after an error by its testing partner gave the model unintended internet access. The incident adds to a ⁠growing list of ⁠cases in ​which AI agents from major developers breached systems at other companies during testing, after Anthropic said last week that some of its models ⁠hacked three companies, and OpenAI disclosed that an AI agent breached the startup Hugging Face. AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be? Read more Meta said a misconfiguration by the independent testing company Irregular inadvertently allowed one ⁠of its models internet access during an evaluation, adding that it was investigating the incident. The model “exploited ​a security vulnerability in a third-party service, ‌in a manner similar ‌to previously reported instances with other companies”, Meta said in a statement. Earlier in the day, ‌The Information, citing sources, reported that Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 model, which it has touted as its most capable model for real-world coding and agentic tasks, breached an unidentified company and altered its internal systems. A spokesperson for Irregular told Reuters the incident was the “exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week” and that it did ‌not involve a “sandbox escape or a sophisticated cyber action”. “There are no current open issues. Irregular is developing a white paper to share best ​practices for containment and securely running cyber evaluations,” Irregular said. The incidents revealed by Meta and Anthropic were due to mistakes that inadvertently gave their models access to the open internet. That contrasts with OpenAI, whose AI agent independently exploited a novel vulnerability to reach the internet during cyber testing. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Preview latest after newsletter promotion Even ⁠so, the breaches highlight how AI has increased threats to cybersecurity and ​how developers can struggle ​to keep the capabilities of their ​models contained. The disclosures are likely to intensify a US government push to ​better manage AI security ‌risks at a ​time when Anthropic and ​OpenAI are racing to release more capable systems ahead of their planned public listings. Prominent leaders at these labs have called for a slowdown to address risks first. Delivered weekdays. Trump’s Flurry of National Security Policies The administration made moves on drones, cyberwarfare, and ship building. By Eli Wizevich , an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy , and Maxine Davey , an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy . U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Aug. 14. U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Aug. 14. Samuel Corum/Getty Images U.S. Foreign Policy Security United States August 14, 2026, 4:17 PM Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the United States ’ new national security directives, a drone incursion into Latvian airspace, and a controversial delay in Zambia ’s election. Policy Action In Washington U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled a slate of national security directives this week, including aggressive tariffs on drones, measures that free U.S. companies to hack on behalf of the government, and changes to Navy policy. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the United States ’ new national security directives, a drone incursion into Latvian airspace, and a controversial delay in Zambia ’s election. Policy Action In Washington U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled a slate of national security directives this week, including aggressive tariffs on drones, measures that free U.S. companies to hack on behalf of the government, and changes to Navy policy. In the name of “securing American drone dominance,” the Trump administration on Friday announced a 100 percent tariff on drones weighing more than 25 kilograms and drones with thermal imaging; a 25 percent tariff on small drones, even those without particular national security concerns; and a 15 percent tariff on drone parts from allies such as the European Union, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. Drones from the United Kingdom will only face a 10 percent tariff. Trump will implement the tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which gives the president a more legally durable tariff strategy for national security risks after the Supreme Court ruled against a different method in February. The White House’s announcement makes no mention of China, but the move is widely seen as attempting to counter Chinese dominance , as drones have become a critical part of modern warfare from Ukraine to Iran to Latin America . In a national security memorandum on Wednesday, Trump also directed the U.S. government to partner with “vetted” private companies to conduct cyberattacks and surveillance against foreign transnational criminal networks that target U.S. citizens. While the announcement does not say which companies might sign on or what their specific missions would be, it establishes a framework for federal government oversight of such activities and sets guardrails against cyberattacks that would cause loss of life or “rise to the level of use of force or armed attack under international law.” The move offloads work from U.S. military and intelligence agency hackers and puts the United States on more equal footing with the likes of Russia, China, and Iran, which have long merged private cyber capabilities with the state. Hackers linked to these governments “have a history of targeting U.S. critical infrastructure,” including recent suspected Iranian cyberattacks on vulnerable U.S. water systems, Foreign Policy ’s Rishi Iyengar and Christina Lu report . However, the directive makes it clear that it only targets criminal groups that are “not an institutional part of a foreign government or wholly operated under a foreign government’s direction.” But some experts warn that Trump’s directive risks inflaming global cyberwarfare and that attributing cyberattacks to specific actors is a fraught undertaking. “People are regularly and willingly wrong on pretty important incidents,” Nick Carr, threat intelligence lead at Microsoft and a former official at the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, wrote on social media. Finally, Trump achieved a longtime goal on Thursday, when he mandated the Navy’s return to steam catapults to launch jet fighters from aircraft carriers, replacing a newer electromagnetic catapult system. The switch could cost billions of dollars . The memo also allows the Navy to outsource building to overseas shipyards and orders the Pentagon to build a fifth naval shipyard for submarines and aircraft carriers. The order comes alongside growing concerns over the strength and health of the U.S. military , including reportedly poor conditions onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln , a depleted drone arsenal, and a loss to Ukrainian troops in a military training exercise earlier this year. Today’s Most Read The Houthis Are Risking Everything for Iran by Fatima Abo Alasrar Mojtaba Khamenei Is Planning for a Long War by Sina Toossi What Does the Mecca Pact Deliver Pakistan? by Michael Kugelman What We’re Following Fire and drones. Ukrainian drones battered Ust-Luga, Russia’s largest Baltic Sea port, on Friday morning, causing a fire and imperiling a key node in Russia’s oil export network. Russian officials claimed that the country’s air defenses shot down 54 Ukrainian drones, that the fires have been put out, and that there are no casualties. But one day of attack may not be the end. In the span of just seven days in March, Ukraine attacked Ust-Luga four times , which, combined with an additional attack on the port of Primorsk, may have cost Russia nearly $1 billion in oil revenues. Earlier this week, long-range Ukrainian drones forced an oil refinery in the Russian city of Orsk, near the border of Kazakhstan, to shut completely for up to six months. NATO jets also shot down a foreign drone over Latvia on Friday. Two Italian jets from a base in Lithuania and two Turkish jets from a base in Estonia responded to the reported violation of Latvian airspace. The Latvian military is searching for debris near the village of Rugaji, around 20 miles from the Russian border. It has yet to confirm the drone’s origin, but Ukrainian drones have previously strayed into Baltic countries accidentally. A spokesperson for the Latvian military blamed “Russian electromagnetic warfare” for such incidents. Zambian election. Zambia’s Electoral Commission temporarily suspended vote-counting in the country’s parliamentary and presidential elections on Friday, citing reports of ballot theft and violence at polling locations. The Electoral Commission resumed counting later in the day and said the final results of the Aug. 13 elections will still be delivered as expected on Monday. Although 14 candidates are vying for the presidency, it is primarily a showdown between incumbent Hakainde Hichilema, who is favored to win a second term, and opposition leader Brian Mundubile. Hichilema was first elected in 2021 and has since steered the copper-rich nation out of a debt crisis. His long-term economic plan to triple Zambia’s copper output has garnered attention from mineral-hungry powers such as China and the United States. But Zambia’s cost-of-living conditions are still dire, and critics charge that Hichilema has silenced dissent. Hichilema called for patience after the vote-counting was suspended. Mundubile condemned the decision and alleged that the ruling party suspended the vote count for its own benefit. “We have serious grounds for concern that the widespread intimidation surrounding this election is being orchestrated and exploited by elements associated with the state in an attempt to interfere with the democratic will of the Zambian people,” Mundubile said in a video posted to social media. In an earlier post , he claimed that “our tabulation indicated that we have won this election.” After vote-counting resumed, Electoral Commission Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis urged candidates to “desist from ​declaring themselves as the winners of these elections” as preliminary counts are released. Focus on the straits. The United Arab Emirates accused Iran on Friday of a “hostile” drone attack on two ships affiliated with the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) in the Strait of Hormuz yesterday. This follows a similar incident last week, in which the UAE accused Iran of attacking an ADNOC tanker. No deaths have been recorded from either incident, according to the UAE’s Foreign Affairs Ministry; Iran has not responded to the accusations. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters on Thursday that the U.S. military can maintain an “indefinite” naval presence in the strait to enforce its blockade of Iranian ports. The commander of Iran’s navy, meanwhile, insisted that Iran has “complete and decisive” control over the strait. “Reality should be seen on the ground, not in the statements and declarations of U.S. officials,” he said in a statement . U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Newsmax on Thursday that new economic measures to pressure Iran will be announced next week. Meanwhile, 13 countries have joined a maritime military coalition founded by Saudi Arabia to safeguard freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden, Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry announced on Thursday. Bahrain, Bangladesh, the Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Pakistan, Qatar, Somalia, Sudan, Turkey, and Yemen have joined so far, with more expected to follow. What in the World? A major typhoon made landfall in southeastern China on Sunday. What marine animal was it named after? A. Orca B. Swordfish C. Lobster D. Dolphin Odds and Ends A person has been fined $5,255 for blasting a foghorn onboard a ship in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago and causing a sleeping polar bear to wake up and move to a different location. According to a statement released by Svalbard’s governor, the act was “intentional” and thus in violation of the Svalbard Environmental Act, which forbids any actions that “needlessly disturb, attract or pursue a polar bear.” Let sleeping bears lie. And the Answer Is… D. Dolphin The storm also triggered rough conditions as far away as the Philippines. Southeast Asia is disproportionately impacted by inclement weather due to a confluence of factors, FP’s Joseph Rachman wrote in Southeast Asia Brief last November. https://www.newswise.com/articles/swimmi.text: Swimming In Rivers And Lakes Linked To Higher Risk Of Stomach Bugs And Rashes Newswise — People swimming in rivers and lakes could be putting themselves at risk of nasty skin conditions and stomach bugs, according to a new study from the University of East Anglia. Researchers found that people who swam in rivers and lakes were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while higher levels of bacteria linked to faecal pollution were associated with an increased risk of stomach bugs. The findings come amid growing public concern over water quality and a boom in open-water swimming. How the research happened Scientists analysed data from 2,368 volunteers who took part in a rare randomised controlled trial at four freshwater bathing sites in Hungary. Participants were randomly assigned either to spend 10 minutes swimming, including at least three full head immersions, or to remain on the shore without entering the water. Prof Paul Hunter, who led on the analysis, said: “We found that swimmers were more than twice as likely to suffer skin ailments such as rashes, ulcers or itching compared with those who stayed dry. “We also found that the risk of gastrointestinal illness increased as levels of E. coli and other viruses that infect bacteria found in the human gut rose in the water, which is indicative of faecal pollution. “This work provides some of the strongest evidence yet that contamination in freshwater recreational sites can translate into real-world illness among bathers. The hidden dangers in seemingly clean water Although all four study sites met European bathing water standards at the time of the trial, scientists still detected an association between higher levels of microbial contamination and sickness. The study found that for each tenfold increase in E. coli concentration, the risk of gastrointestinal illness rose by around 73 per cent, while higher levels of viruses known as somatic coliphages were associated with a 45 per cent increase in risk. The team say these organisms appear to be better indicators of illness risk in rivers and lakes than intestinal enterococci - a bacteria group currently emphasised in some international water-quality guidance. They also noted that freshwater and coastal waters may require different standards as the behaviour of bacterial indicators differs between the two environments. Swimmers itch One intriguing finding was that skin complaints increased among swimmers regardless of measured levels of faecal indicators. “This could be due to exposure to naturally occurring organisms not linked to sewage pollution,” said Prof Hunter. “One possibility is cercarial dermatitis, commonly known as ‘swimmer's itch’, which is caused by parasites shed by waterfowl that can penetrate human skin and trigger an itchy rash. “Agricultural or industrial contaminants may also play a role,” he added. Growing relevance for UK swimmers The findings add fuel to the debate over the condition of Britain's rivers and lakes. Open-water swimming has surged in popularity in recent years, with advocates praising the mental and physical health benefits of spending time in natural ‘blue spaces’. But campaigners have repeatedly raised concerns about sewage discharges and pollution affecting popular bathing locations. “Our results were consistent across the four Hungarian study sites, which differed in water quality and water types. Our results were also consistent with a previous study in Germany. So overall, this suggests that the relationships that we have identified are generalisable and likely applicable in UK waters,” said Prof Hunter. “But it is important to remember that the rates of illness were relatively low overall and most illnesses were mild and short lived,” he added. “Just over two per cent of participants developed gastrointestinal illness and a similar proportion experienced skin ailments. Respiratory, ear and eye infections were rare.” Nevertheless, the team concluded that higher concentrations of E. coli and related indicators were clearly associated with greater risks of stomach illness, providing evidence that monitoring these microbes remains important for protecting public health. This project was a collaboration of partners from several European institutions, known as Epibathe. The Epibathe projects investigated the risks associated with both marine and freshwater sites. Hungary was chosen for the inland water studies because of the availability of good study sites and experienced local researchers. This final analysis was led by the University of East Anglia. The study was funded by the EU’s 6 th Research Framework Programme, and by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), in partnership with the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). ‘A Randomised Controlled Trial Assessing Infectious Disease Risks from Bathing in Inland Recreational Waters’ is published in the International Journal of Hygiene and Environmental Health. https://www.uea.ac.uk/about/news/article/the-hearts-natural-bypass-that-could-spare-patients-from-ri...
